Record version: 1.0. Owner: fixture author. Recorded: 2026-11-23. Status: attributed public background, not Flint Ledger operating policy. Every Flint Ledger and Meridian Works business record, person, amount, technical finding and candidate in this dossier is synthetic. The fictional decision cutoff is 2025-05-14 12:00 UTC; retrieval in 2026 does not move that cutoff or establish historical contractual terms.

S01: GitLab's February 1, 2017 account of its database incident described accidental production deletion and recovery from a roughly six-hour-old backup. It distinguished affected database metadata from unaffected Git repositories and wikis, and reported that several intended backup or replication mechanisms were unreliable or absent. This was an evolving company report with a later postmortem link, not an independent audit or a universal statement about present GitLab recovery capability.

S02: GitHub's October 30, 2018 analysis of its October 21 incident described choosing data integrity over faster restoration of usability. It discussed backup transfer and validation work, divergent writes needing reconciliation, and recovery estimates that missed important variables. The page reports an overall no-user-data-loss outcome while also describing continuing manual reconciliation. The retrieved page carries a December 19, 2021 update. That later account does not determine what any fictional operator could know during an unresolved recovery.

S03: Atlassian's April 29, 2022 post-incident review described an accidental site deletion event, recovery involving multiple dependent stores and identity mappings, and restoration approaches that changed during the incident. It acknowledged communication shortcomings, including a need to disclose known facts and unknowns earlier. Its eventual restoration and limited-loss statements describe that historical event, not a recovery guarantee for a different service or a basis for importing its SLA into this dossier.

No transcript reuse permission has been verified. These paragraphs are independently authored factual paraphrases with attribution; zero source words are presented as quotations. The sources motivate separate questions about backup existence, recoverability, application consistency and useful communication under uncertainty. # E02 — Account order and project workflow

Record version: ORD-7.2. Owner: account operations analyst Lena Voss. Effective order: 2024-05-16. Account snapshot: 2025-05-14 09:15 UTC. Status: signed fictional order plus verified account inventory; no new recovery consent.

Meridian Works pays Flint Ledger $2,400 monthly for 180 named users and 24 project workspaces. The current month was charged and settled on May 1. Service includes document revision references, structured approval records and export tools. Raw engineering files live in the attachment object store, but an object without its project relationship and revision record may be unusable for evidentiary purposes. The ordinary subscription does not promise that a folder listing is a complete approval register. A separate Recovery Assist feature provides customer-scheduled exports; Meridian never purchased or enabled it. That fact does not remove Flint Ledger's own backup and service responsibilities.

The affected workspace is Bridge Pack, identifier MW-B17. Twenty-three other workspaces remain available and are under a change restriction only for operations using the same cleanup mechanism. A tenant-wide restore would replace their current metadata too. Account administration lists Sera Bell as the commercial owner and tender director, and Owen Dale as the technical administrator permitted to authorize a sandbox export. Owen may not waive compensation claims, accept revised subscription terms, or authorize production replacement of approval history. Sera can approve a production cutover after receiving a written impact description; no cutover consent exists in this snapshot.

Bridge Pack contains the company's submission evidence for a regional public-works tender. The signed account order does not mention this tender, a guaranteed launch date, or a fixed loss payment if the customer misses a bid. The service knew about the tender through the account team in April. Meridian's internal tender ID and all people in these records are invented. The external tender portal is not operated by Flint Ledger. A support action cannot extend its cutoff or certify a submission on behalf of the procuring organization.

Normal connectors synchronize document revisions, send approval invitations and update a client dashboard every ten minutes. Those actions have side effects beyond database writes: an old invitation can be emailed twice and a late revision can replace a document pointer in the dashboard. Disabling only browser editing does not stop them. The incident commander has disabled these connectors for MW-B17 and preserved their queues. Work on unaffected workspaces continues, so a blanket account freeze would interrupt live delivery without improving the affected backup chain.

Meridian has asked for both a usable record and an explanation of the loss. Its current invoice is not overdue and no collection action is pending. No retention offer, annual contract or release has been accepted. This inventory establishes account and role scopes; it does not attest that the latest backup is complete or that the customer agrees to any particular recovery method.
# E03 — Customer thread and tender deadlines

Record version: MW-THREAD.3. Owner: support owner Ellis Rowan. Thread snapshot: 2025-05-14 10:35 UTC. Status: authenticated customer statements; tender consequences remain customer-reported except where the portal receipt is transcribed.

At 07:12 Sera reported that Bridge Pack showed empty approval panels and several broken revision links. She asked support to stop changes that could make the situation worse. At 07:24 a support associate replied that the backup was complete and the workspace should be back within two hours. Sera arranged staff around a 09:30 recovery. At 09:42, after no usable workspace arrived, she asked why Sales still called the service loss-proof and why the incident banner said only that some users were seeing delays. The team has acknowledged receiving these messages but has not sent a substantive correction of the two-hour assurance.

Sera's board briefing starts at 14:00 UTC today. She needs a written operational status by 13:00 to tell the board whether to use the manual submission pack, request a portal exception, or continue waiting for Flint Ledger. She will not accept another unqualified restoration time. Her preferred outcome is the latest complete approval history, but she says a properly labeled older baseline might still help staff identify gaps. That statement is an expression of usefulness, not consent to overwrite the live workspace or to represent old approvals as current.

The transcribed portal receipt shows the tender closes May 14 at 17:00 UTC. It recommends completing upload by 16:30 because the package takes up to thirty minutes to process. At 10:10 Meridian asked the procuring organization whether a supporting evidence supplement could follow later. No response had arrived by 10:35. Sera has not claimed that an extension is granted. A tender extension cannot be promised by Flint Ledger, and staff should not infer that requesting one makes today's deadline disappear.

Owen's team can spend the morning reconciling exports if a reliable baseline is available. Two engineers leave for a safety inspection at 15:00; the remaining tender administrator can check filenames and upload packages but cannot recreate engineering approval decisions. Meridian has local document files and some emailed signoffs. The number and authority of missing signoffs are addressed in later records, not established by this initial customer count. Asking for all material again would consume the same people needed to complete the bid.

Sera requests reimbursement of $18,000 already committed to an external document-control team and protection against an estimated $120,000 lost tender opportunity. She has not supplied a final invoice or proof that the tender is lost. She also asks that no annual renewal be processed while the recovery is unresolved. She authorizes incident evidence preservation and a named recovery contact. She expressly withholds permission for production rollback, automatic re-sending of approval invitations, or closing the support case after a service credit.
# E04 — Current incident state and accepted writes

Record version: IR-619.4. Owner: incident commander Drina Cole. Snapshot: 2025-05-14 11:20 UTC. Status: preliminary internal findings; preservation complete, final cause report pending.

At 06:42 UTC a Flint Ledger maintenance job removed metadata associations for workspace MW-B17. The job was intended to clear expired preview workspaces. Its tenant resolver selected the production workspace after a configuration mapping error. The evidence supports a service-side maintenance action; no current record supports saying Meridian deleted its own project. The precise review and deployment failures remain under investigation. Security has found no indication of unauthorized access in the retained control-plane records, but the investigation is about data integrity, and that limited observation does not certify all historical access.

At 06:45 Meridian's connector submitted 74 changes. The API issued success responses for those requests before the write fence completed at 06:51. The requests include 21 new document revision pointers, 31 approval transitions and 22 comments. Their receipt journal and payload digests are preserved. A success response establishes acceptance, not that every associated attachment and downstream event can be reconstructed from the journal. The team has not applied those writes to a restored workspace and must not describe them as already recovered. Some refer to document versions absent from the oldest backup.

At 06:51 the incident commander fenced writes, paused outgoing invitations and isolated the affected workspace. The tenant's other 23 workspaces remain writable and current. Copies of the damaged metadata database, queue state, object inventory and relevant access configuration were sealed at 07:08 under receipt PR-619. The collection is restricted to incident staff. A clone may be built from these copies; destructive repair on the only surviving damaged database is prohibited. Retention has been extended through June 13 regardless of any subscription cancellation.

The current interface is an incident page with a support contact. It does not expose old records as though they were current. The unmodified damaged state is retained offline and cannot be used as a writable customer workspace. A read-only recovered clone requires separate identity and relation checks before customer access, even if its database starts normally. There is no emergency requiring the customer to choose a destructive restore immediately to save the evidence.

The scope count of missing records is provisional. A dashboard screenshot showing zero approvals is an application symptom, not proof that every approval row is physically gone. Surviving object bytes do not establish that the revision-to-approval relationships remain valid. Drina owns operational recovery and can authorize isolated tests under the current policy. Ellis owns customer updates. Finance decisions and acceptance of a potentially older production state belong to different roles and cannot be supplied by the incident commander merely to shorten the outage.
# E05 — Current recovery control policy

Record version: REC-4.1. Owner: reliability director Anika Shaw. Effective: 2025-04-01. Status: current mandatory operating control for customer data repair; fictional policy.

A restore is a controlled data change, not a ticket status. Operators must preserve the damaged state and any accepted post-snapshot writes before repair. A recovered database must be restored first into an isolated environment with outbound connectors disabled. The operator records source snapshot, application version, encryption-key references, table and object counts, relation checks and the known recovery-point gap. A successful backup job or database startup alone is not evidence that the application can reconstruct a coherent customer workspace.

The incident commander can approve non-destructive isolated restoration tests and prepare a read-only extract for the existing authorized account administrators. Test costs and customer access must remain within the incident and privacy controls. No production tenant replacement is permitted until the technical owner records validation and the commercial account owner receives a plain explanation of lost or uncertain changes, downtime, identifier effects and rollback limits. The authorized customer must explicitly consent to the described cutover. A customer's request to recover data is not consent to silently discard accepted later writes.

Recovery tests must use a copy. Operators may not delete surviving media, expire incident journals, rewrite source backups or resume automated queues just to make a test pass. When replaying journals, compare record identity and application semantics; repeated approval transitions and invitation deliveries are not harmless duplicates. Separate technically replayable events from events requiring customer verification. Original timestamps may be preserved where supported, but staff may not invent an approval signature or backdate a manually recreated decision to make a package appear complete.

Recovery-point and recovery-time objectives are planning measures, not promises for every loss mechanism. Contractual service terms may include separate obligations and remedies. Staff must distinguish an estimate of copy completion from validation, customer review and release to production. If a published estimate changes, communicate what has changed and the next controllable checkpoint. Final root cause is not a prerequisite to sending a useful interim status. When no completion estimate is sufficiently supported, state the uncertainty and identify the work that could narrow it.

The customer incident owner must coordinate engineering, support and commercial records, including deadlines outside the service. A credit does not close a recovery or information request. Work on mitigation and evidence preservation continues while liability or compensation is reviewed. Recovery priority is based on operational impact and safe resource use; a new purchase, renewal or public silence must not be a prerequisite for ordinary incident recovery. An optional paid feature may be described for future use only with accurate scope and without implying it can retroactively create missing data.

This policy supersedes REC-2.6 for tenant-level data repair after April 1. Historical playbooks may supply technical clues, but their shortcuts do not grant present execution authority. The approval register records case-specific spending and customer permissions separately from this control policy.
# E06 — Archived fast-recovery playbook and failed drill

Record version: REC-2.6. Owner: platform operations archive. Issued: 2024-08-19. Superseded: 2025-04-01 by REC-4.1. Archive annotation recorded: 2025-05-14 08:05 UTC. Status: historical training material; not current cutover authority.

The archived playbook describes replacing a single-workspace database from the newest completed snapshot, restarting the web service and asking the customer to report discrepancies. Its triage card used a two-hour target from snapshot selection to web availability. That number came from a small test tenant without attachment history, customer connectors or recent accepted writes. It did not cover a real tender evidence bundle, relation reconstruction or human approval review. The old card was still present in the support macro library this morning and appears to be the source of the 07:24 support promise.

The old procedure advised temporarily disabling browser edits but allowed background synchronizers to reconnect as the service restarted. In a March 12 drill, the browser looked healthy while a restarted connector delivered duplicate approval requests and replaced two newer document pointers with old values. The drill found no issue with raw object availability, yet the approval register could not be reconciled automatically. A green web-health check therefore measured a narrower property than recovery of business records. The drill did not involve Meridian or any customer data.

A second problem was identifier handling. Test restores generated new workspace and document identifiers while some exports retained original identifiers. Downstream systems then treated recovered records as new documents. Staff manually mapped a small sample but did not prove the mapping for a tenant of Meridian's size. REC-4.1 now requires documenting these relationships and disables outbound effects during testing. The archive can still help engineers find the location of snapshot manifests; it cannot authorize ignoring those newer controls.

The training slide also suggested a standard $500 service credit as an immediate apology. That was the support limit for fee adjustments and never authorized consequential-loss compensation. A handwritten presenter note saying managers can sort out the rest referred to escalation, not an unlimited delegated budget. There is no evidence that the customer saw or accepted this internal playbook. It cannot reduce obligations in the signed order or bind the customer to an older recovery point.

At 08:05 the reliability director removed this playbook from active incident links and asked Support Operations to disable the two-hour macro. The archive copy is retained because it helps explain the premature promise and system history. No corrected macro has yet been sent to Meridian. Reviewing this artifact should not distract engineering from the current chain and relation checks. It identifies where an outdated estimate came from, rather than proving that all existing backups are unusable or that a two-hour repair can never be safe for a different incident.
# E07 — Backup inventory and limits of verification

Record version: BK-619.3. Owner: database recovery lead Jules Marin. Snapshot: 2025-05-14 10:50 UTC. Status: observed inventory and incomplete tests; latest complete application recovery point not established.

Backup N-011 is a full database snapshot from May 14 01:00 UTC. Its file digest matches the backup manifest and a scratch database opens successfully. Table-level checks match the recorded row counts for document and approval metadata. The attachment index points to 96,420 objects. An inventory comparison finds bytes for 96,372 references and 48 unresolved references, many associated with retired previews. The team has not yet determined whether any of those 48 are needed for Bridge Pack's tender. A verified metadata snapshot is useful, but not a complete application-level attestation.

Incremental jobs report successful upload through 06:40. Their top-level status measures completion of the upload task and is green. The manifest for the 05:10–05:20 interval references a segment not found in the usual bucket listing. An archive index references a second storage location; Jules has requested a privileged retrieval check, due at 12:45. No operator has yet produced or replayed that segment. Without it the team cannot represent the full incremental chain as continuous. Later segments may contain useful records but cannot simply be concatenated into an intact history.

Replica R-2 is at 06:43 but already contains the cleanup effect. Its newer timestamp does not make it a clean pre-incident recovery source. It is retained for comparison and possible surviving relationships. The preproduction copy is from May 12 and excludes production attachments; it cannot supply yesterday's signoffs. A customer export from May 13 is a separate artifact described in E10. None of these copies should be deleted after selecting a preferred working source.

Encryption keys needed for N-011 are available through the normal operations service. Access is restricted and the key material is not copied into support tickets or this dossier. A key being available does not resolve the missing incremental segment. The jobs' retention policy normally deletes temporary staging data at 18:00 today, but the incident commander recorded a preservation override at 09:55 for all listed sources. No deadline forces destruction today. Jules verified the override in the scheduler at 10:10 and included its receipt with PR-619.

The recovery team can start an N-011 isolated clone now while the archive retrieval proceeds. They have one dedicated database engineer and one application engineer through 15:00, with additional capacity afterward. A separate export worker is available if assigned by 12:15. The team has not yet committed that worker or started a customer-facing extract. Backup monitoring and the known gap are also assigned to the reliability review. A future monitoring fix cannot create the missing segment retroactively or establish a present recovery promise.
# E08 — Recovery estimates with incompatible scopes

Record version: EST-619.2. Owner: incident program manager Tavi Ross. Consolidated: 2025-05-14 11:10 UTC. Status: working estimates, not committed completion times; all times UTC.

At 08:20 database engineer Jules estimated six hours to restore N-011 after allocation of a database host. That estimate covered transfer, decompression, database start and basic table checks. The host became available at 09:00, so a literal six-hour projection would end at 15:00. It did not include attachment relationships, replay of the 74 accepted changes, application identity checks, customer validation or production release. Record version: REC-4.1. Owner: reliability director Anika Shaw. Effective: 2025-04-01. Status: current mandatory operating control for customer data repair; fictional policy.

A restore is a controlled data change, not a ticket status. Operators must preserve the damaged state and any accepted post-snapshot writes before repair. A recovered database must be restored first into an isolated environment with outbound connectors disabled. The operator records source snapshot, application version, encryption-key references, table and object counts, relation checks and the known recovery-point gap. The incident commander can approve non-destructive isolated restoration tests and prepare a read-only extract for the existing authorized account administrators. Test costs and customer access must remain within the incident and privacy controls. No production tenant replacement is permitted until the technical owner records validation and the commercial account owner receives a plain explanation of lost or uncertain changes, downtime, identifier effects and rollback limits. The authorized customer must explicitly consent to the described cutover. A customer's request to recover data is not consent to silently discard accepted later writes.

Recovery tests must use a copy. Operators may not delete surviving media, expire incident journals, rewrite source backups or resume automated queues just to make a test pass. When replaying journals, compare record identity and application semantics; repeated approval transitions and invitation deliveries are not harmless duplicates. Separate technically replayable events from events requiring customer verification. Original timestamps may be preserved where supported, but staff may not invent an approval signature or backdate a manually recreated decision to make a package appear complete.

Recovery-point and recovery-time objectives are planning measures, not promises for every loss mechanism. Contractual service terms may include separate obligations and remedies. Staff must distinguish an estimate of copy completion from validation, customer review and release to production. If a published estimate changes, communicate what has changed and the next controllable checkpoint. Final root cause is not a prerequisite to sending a useful interim status. When no completion estimate is sufficiently supported, state the uncertainty and identify the work that could narrow it.

The customer incident owner must coordinate engineering, support and commercial records, including deadlines outside the service. A credit does not close a recovery or information request. Work on mitigation and evidence preservation continues while liability or compensation is reviewed. Recovery priority is based on operational impact and safe resource use; a new purchase, renewal or public silence must not be a prerequisite for ordinary incident recovery. An optional paid feature may be described for future use only with accurate scope and without implying it can retroactively create missing data.

This policy supersedes REC-2.6 for tenant-level data repair after April 1. Historical playbooks may supply technical clues, but their shortcuts do not grant present execution authority.
